Glaucoma and angle closure
Reference note
Voice viva take-home
Written by Eye Academy
Revised November 2026
About this note
This note was written by Eye Academy for the developer take-home task. It is a revision summary for
trainees, not clinical guidance: always follow local protocols and current national guidance. Page
numbers are printed at the foot of each page so that answers can cite them.
Aqueous humour and intraocular pressure
Aqueous humour is secreted by the non-pigmented epithelium of the ciliary body, mostly by active
transport (with smaller contributions from ultrafiltration and diffusion), at roughly 2 to 3 microlitres per
minute. It passes from the posterior chamber through the pupil into the anterior chamber, then leaves
the eye by two routes.
Conventional (trabecular) outflow. Aqueous passes through the trabecular meshwork into
Schlemm's canal, then into collector channels and the episcleral veins. This route carries most of the
outflow in adults and depends on pressure.
Uveoscleral outflow. Aqueous passes through the ciliary muscle into the suprachoroidal space. This
route is largely independent of pressure, is relatively larger in younger people, and is the main target
of prostaglandin analogues.
Intraocular pressure (IOP) reflects the balance between production and outflow. In adults the population
average is about 15 to 16 mmHg, and 21 mmHg (about two standard deviations above the mean) is often
quoted as the upper limit of normal, but many people with glaucoma have pressures below this and many
people above it never develop damage. IOP varies through the day and is often highest in the early
morning.
Measuring IOP
Goldmann applanation tonometry at the slit lamp is the reference standard. It assumes an average
central corneal thickness (CCT): a thick cornea makes the reading higher than the true pressure, and a
thin cornea makes it lower. Record the time of measurement, the method and which eye. Rebound and
non-contact tonometers are useful for screening and for children but are less accurate at very high
pressures.

Assessing the drainage angle
Van Herick grading
With a thin, bright slit beam offset about 60 degrees from the microscope and placed at the temporal
limbus, compare the depth of the most peripheral anterior chamber with the thickness of the cornea.
Grade
Peripheral chamber depth
Interpretation
4
Equal to or greater than corneal thickness
Wide open
3
Between a quarter and a half
Closure unlikely
2
A quarter
Needs gonioscopy
1
Less than a quarter
Angle usually dangerously narrow on gonioscopy
Van Herick is a screening test only. It can overestimate angle width, particularly in plateau iris
configuration, so grades 1 and 2 (and any clinical suspicion) should be confirmed with gonioscopy.
Gonioscopy
Gonioscopy is the reference standard for seeing the angle structures directly. Use a dark room and a
short, thin slit beam that avoids the pupil, because light constricts the pupil and can open an angle that
would be closed in the dark (this happens in about a third of appositionally closed angles). From
posterior to anterior the visible structures are the ciliary body band, scleral spur, trabecular meshwork
and Schwalbe's line. The angle is usually narrowest superiorly.
Indentation (dynamic) gonioscopy with a four-mirror lens pushes aqueous into the angle. If the iris
falls back, the closure is appositional; if it stays stuck to the meshwork, there are peripheral anterior
synechiae (PAS).
Iridotrabecular contact (ITC) means the peripheral iris touches the posterior (pigmented)
trabecular meshwork. ITC for at least 180 degrees is the threshold used by the American Academy of
Ophthalmology and in recent trials. The original international (ISGEO) definition, still used in Kanski,
requires three or more quadrants (270 degrees).
Shaffer grading records the angle width in each quadrant: grade 4 (35 to 45 degrees, ciliary body
visible), grade 3 (scleral spur visible), grade 2 (trabecular meshwork but not scleral spur visible),
grade 1 (only Schwalbe's line and perhaps the top of the meshwork visible), slit, and grade 0 (closed).
Anterior segment OCT and ultrasound biomicroscopy (UBM) give images of the angle and complement
gonioscopy, but they do not replace it. UBM is better for plateau iris and other ciliary body causes,
because it can see behind the iris.
Primary angle closure
Terminology
The terms below follow the international (ISGEO) classification used by the major guidelines.

Primary angle closure suspect (PACS): ITC for at least 180 degrees, with normal IOP, no PAS and no
glaucomatous optic neuropathy.
Primary angle closure (PAC): ITC with raised IOP and/or PAS, but a healthy optic disc and visual field.
Other signs of previous closure, such as iris whorling or sectoral atrophy, glaukomflecken or excess
trabecular pigment, support the diagnosis.
Primary angle closure glaucoma (PACG): angle closure with glaucomatous optic neuropathy.
Acute primary angle closure (APAC): a sudden symptomatic rise in IOP caused by angle closure,
called an acute angle-closure crisis in the American guidance. It can occur at any point along this
spectrum.
Subacute (intermittent) angle closure: milder, spontaneously resolving episodes, often relieved by
bright light or sleep, which both constrict the pupil.
Risk factors
Hypermetropia and short axial length (nanophthalmos, below 20 mm, carries particular risk)
Older age, as the lens thickens and moves forward
Female sex
East Asian or Inuit ethnicity
A family history of angle closure
A shallow anterior chamber and a thick or anteriorly placed lens
Mechanisms
Mechanisms are grouped by the level at which they act, from the iris backwards. More than one is often
present (mixed mechanism).
Pupil block. Contact between the iris and lens slows the flow of aqueous through the pupil. Pressure
builds behind the iris, which bows forward (iris bombé) and closes the angle. This is the most
common mechanism and is relieved by a peripheral iridotomy.
Plateau iris and a thick peripheral iris roll. The ciliary processes sit anteriorly and push the
peripheral iris into the angle, even though the central chamber may look reasonably deep. Non-pupilblock mechanisms are relatively more important in East Asian patients. See the plateau iris section
below.
Lens factor. A thick or forward lens crowds the anterior segment. Removing the lens deepens the
chamber and opens the angle. Closure that is mainly lens-driven (phacomorphic or a subluxed lens)
is usually classed as secondary.
Acute primary angle closure
Symptoms
Sudden, severe, aching pain in one eye, often with a frontal headache on the same side. About 5% of
attacks affect both eyes at once.
Blurred vision and coloured haloes around lights, caused by corneal oedema

Nausea, vomiting and sometimes abdominal pain, which can lead to a mistaken diagnosis of an
abdominal or neurological problem
Earlier, milder episodes that resolved on their own, often in the evening or after time in dim light
Signs
Reduced visual acuity, often 6/60 to hand movements
Very high IOP, usually 50 to 80 mmHg (almost always above 40 mmHg)
Ciliary injection (violaceous redness most marked around the limbus)
Corneal epithelial oedema, often with a hazy view of the iris and fundus
A shallow peripheral anterior chamber, usually with flare
A fixed, mid-dilated, often vertically oval pupil, caused by ischaemia of the iris sphincter
A hyperaemic, swollen optic disc if the fundus can be seen
A narrow angle in the other eye, which is an important diagnostic clue. If the fellow angle is open, look
hard for a secondary cause.
After the attack: an initially low IOP (ciliary body shutdown), folds in Descemet membrane,
glaukomflecken (small white anterior subcapsular lens opacities), spiral iris atrophy, an irregular or
fixed pupil, posterior synechiae and PAS, and optic disc pallor with or without cupping
Triggers
Attacks are often triggered by things that dilate the pupil into the mid-position, where pupil block is
greatest.
Dim light, such as a cinema or a dark room
Emotional stress
A semi-prone position, such as reading, which lets the lens move forward
Dilating drops, including tropicamide and phenylephrine
Drugs with anticholinergic effects, including some antihistamines (for example chlorphenamine),
tricyclic antidepressants, antispasmodics, hyoscine travel-sickness patches and some inhaled
bronchodilators (such as nebulised ipratropium)
Sympathomimetic drugs, including decongestants and cold and flu remedies
Rarely, strong miotics, which can pull the lens-iris diaphragm forward
Drug-induced bilateral angle closure from topiramate and some sulfonamide-type drugs works by a
different mechanism and is covered under secondary angle closure.

Managing an acute attack
The aims are to lower the IOP quickly, relieve pupil block, protect the other eye and prevent a recurrence.
Treatment below is an outline only; doses and choices should follow local protocols.
Immediate treatment
Position and support. Lie the patient flat (supine) to let the lens fall back, and give analgesia and an
antiemetic.
Topical IOP-lowering drops. A beta-blocker such as timolol 0.5% (unless the patient has asthma,
COPD, bradycardia or heart block) and an alpha-agonist such as apraclonidine 1% or brimonidine
0.2%. A topical carbonic anhydrase inhibitor can be added. Leave 3 to 5 minutes between drops.
Prostaglandin analogues act too slowly to help in the acute phase.
Topical steroid. Prednisolone acetate 1% to reduce inflammation.
Pilocarpine. Pilocarpine 2% constricts the pupil and pulls the iris away from the angle. The iris
sphincter is often ischaemic and does not respond while the IOP is very high, so pilocarpine works
better once the pressure has started to fall (many protocols wait until the IOP is below 40 to 50
mmHg). Avoid repeated intensive doses and strong concentrations such as 4%, which can push the
lens-iris diaphragm forward and cause systemic toxicity.
Fellow eye. Many units give pilocarpine 1% to the other eye until it has an iridotomy, although some
specialists avoid this. Either way, the priority is prompt iridotomy in both eyes.
Systemic carbonic anhydrase inhibitor. Acetazolamide 500 mg, given intravenously if the IOP is
above about 50 mmHg or the patient is vomiting, otherwise orally (not the slow-release form), then

250 mg four times a day. Check for sulfonamide allergy, kidney disease, low potassium and sickle cell
disease before giving it. Do not use it when the angle closure is caused by topiramate or another
sulfonamide drug.
Hyperosmotic agents if the pressure stays high: intravenous mannitol 20%, or oral glycerol 50%
(avoid glycerol in people with diabetes; oral isosorbide is an alternative). Watch for heart failure, fluid
overload and kidney problems.
Recheck the IOP every 30 to 60 minutes. Indenting the central cornea with a gonioscopy lens or a squint
hook can push aqueous into the angle and help break the attack. Topical glycerol can clear corneal
epithelial oedema first, which improves the view and reduces the risk of abrasion.
If the IOP does not fall
Review the diagnosis, for example aqueous misdirection or a secondary cause
Early laser iridotomy, after clearing the cornea with topical glycerol
Laser peripheral iridoplasty to pull the peripheral iris away from the angle, particularly if the cornea is
too cloudy for an iridotomy or systemic carbonic anhydrase inhibitors must be avoided
Anterior chamber paracentesis as a temporary measure. It works quickly but the effect is short-lived
and there is a small risk of damage to the lens.
Surgical peripheral iridectomy, early lens extraction (with or without goniosynechialysis),
trabeculectomy or cyclodiode, ideally in a specialist glaucoma unit
Definitive treatment
Laser peripheral iridotomy (LPI) in the affected eye once the cornea has cleared, usually within a
few days. Continue topical steroid for at least a week.
Prophylactic LPI in the fellow eye, because without treatment around 40 to 50% of fellow eyes have
an attack within 5 to 10 years (higher figures are reported in some series). Long-term pilocarpine is
not an adequate alternative.
Lens extraction is an alternative or addition to LPI, particularly when the lens is thick or cataractous,
and there should be a low threshold for it after an attack. In the EAGLE trial, clear lens extraction in
people aged 50 or over with PAC (IOP 30 mmHg or more) or PACG gave better pressure control and
quality of life than LPI, and was cost-effective. EAGLE did not study eyes during or straight after an
acute attack.
Follow-up
Once the eye has settled, repeat gonioscopy (including the affected eye, which could not be assessed
properly during the attack), examine both optic discs and arrange visual field testing. Check that the
iridotomies are patent. Some eyes develop chronically raised IOP from PAS or trabecular damage and
need long-term medical or surgical treatment. Any trigger drug should be stopped and the patient
warned about others.

Laser peripheral iridotomy
An iridotomy is a small full-thickness opening in the peripheral iris that lets aqueous bypass the pupil. It
equalises the pressure in front of and behind the iris and relieves pupil block.
Indications
After acute primary angle closure, in both eyes
Primary angle closure and primary angle closure glaucoma
Selected primary angle closure suspects. The ZAP and ANA-LIG trials showed only a small protective
effect, so LPI is usually reserved for higher-risk people: symptoms of intermittent closure, a need for
drugs that may cause pupil block, frequent dilated examinations (for example diabetic retinopathy or
AMD), poor access to eye care, or a family history of angle closure.
Pigment dispersion with marked reverse pupil block (less commonly used now)
Technique
Pre-treat with pilocarpine to stretch and thin the iris and with apraclonidine to reduce the post-laser
pressure spike. Place the opening in the peripheral iris, ideally in an iris crypt, either fully covered by the
upper lid or temporally, using a contact lens to focus the beam. Avoid the lid margin and tear meniscus,
where a partly covered opening is most likely to cause visual symptoms. The Nd:YAG laser is used most
often; argon laser can be added first in thick, dark irides to reduce bleeding and the energy needed.
Complications
A temporary rise in IOP, so recheck the pressure after about an hour
Bleeding from the iris or a small hyphaema, usually stopped by gentle pressure with the contact lens
Anterior uveitis
Visual disturbance such as lines, glare or ghost images, particularly if the opening is only partly
covered by the lid
Corneal epithelial or endothelial burns, especially in a shallow chamber
Closure of the opening, needing repeat treatment
Persistent angle closure despite a patent iridotomy, which suggests plateau iris or a lens mechanism
Rarely, aqueous misdirection or damage to the lens or retina
Plateau iris
In plateau iris the ciliary processes are positioned anteriorly and hold the peripheral iris forward. The
central anterior chamber can look normal or only slightly shallow, while the iris surface is flat and the
peripheral angle is narrow. Patients tend to be younger than those with pure pupil block.
Plateau iris configuration describes the anatomy seen on gonioscopy or imaging.
Plateau iris syndrome describes an angle that stays closed, or closes again, despite a patent
iridotomy. Darkness or dilation may be needed to show it. In the complete form the IOP rises; in the
incomplete form the closure is less extensive and the IOP stays normal.

Gonioscopy shows a "double hump" sign on indentation: a central hump from the iris over the lens and a
peripheral hump from the iris over the ciliary processes. Ultrasound biomicroscopy confirms the anterior
ciliary processes. Laser iridoplasty is the procedure of choice when the angle stays closed after
iridotomy; other options are long-term pilocarpine and lens extraction.
Secondary angle closure
Secondary angle closure has an identifiable cause other than primary anatomy. It can be divided into
causes that push the iris forward from behind and causes that pull it into the angle from in front. It is
more often one-sided than primary angle closure.
Pushing mechanisms
Phacomorphic or lens subluxation. A swollen cataractous lens, or a lens that has moved forward
(for example after trauma, or in pseudoexfoliation or microspherophakia), pushes the iris forward.
Treated by lowering the IOP and removing the lens.
Ciliochoroidal effusion. Drugs such as topiramate, and some other sulfonamide-type drugs, cause
fluid to collect around the ciliary body, which rotates forward. Typically both eyes are affected within
the first two weeks of starting the drug, with a sudden myopic shift. Stop the drug (with the
prescriber) and use cycloplegics, topical steroid and IOP-lowering drops. Avoid acetazolamide, which
is itself a sulfonamide. Pilocarpine and iridotomy do not help, because there is no pupil block, and
pilocarpine can make it worse. Effusions also occur after extensive panretinal photocoagulation, in
nanophthalmos and with a central retinal vein occlusion.
Aqueous misdirection (malignant glaucoma). Usually after eye surgery, especially in short eyes
with angle closure, aqueous flows backwards into the vitreous and pushes the lens and iris forward.
Both the central and peripheral chamber become flat despite a patent iridotomy. Treated with
cycloplegics, aqueous suppressants and hyperosmotics, avoiding miotics; then, if needed, Nd:YAG
laser to the anterior hyaloid face (in pseudophakic eyes), cyclodiode or vitrectomy.
Posterior segment causes, such as large tumours, haemorrhage, a large serous retinal detachment,
expanding gas or silicone oil after vitrectomy, or a tight scleral buckle.
Pulling mechanisms
Neovascular glaucoma. A fibrovascular membrane grows over the angle after retinal ischaemia, for
example from diabetes or central retinal vein occlusion. The angle is open at first, then the membrane
contracts to zip the angle shut. Treat the ischaemia (anti-VEGF injections and panretinal
photocoagulation) as well as the IOP.
Uveitis. Inflammation leads to PAS, often inferiorly, and posterior synechiae can cause pupil block
and iris bombé.
Iridocorneal endothelial (ICE) syndrome, in which abnormal corneal endothelium migrates over the
angle, often producing high PAS that reach beyond Schwalbe's line.
Epithelial or fibrous downgrowth, after surgery or a penetrating injury.

Primary open-angle glaucoma and ocular hypertension
Primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) is a chronic, progressive optic neuropathy with characteristic
optic disc cupping and visual field loss, in an eye with an open angle and no secondary cause. It is usually
painless and found at a routine eye test. Risk factors include raised IOP, older age, black African or
Caribbean ethnicity, a family history, myopia and a thin central cornea.
Ocular hypertension (OHT) means an IOP above 21 mmHg with a healthy optic disc and visual field. In the
UK, NICE guidance (NG81, updated 2022) recommends offering treatment when the IOP is 24 mmHg or
more and the person is at risk of visual impairment in their lifetime. For both OHT and POAG, 360-degree
selective laser trabeculoplasty (SLT) is now offered first, with a generic prostaglandin analogue as the
usual first-choice medicine if SLT is unsuitable or not wanted. This change followed the LiGHT trial.
Normal-tension glaucoma describes glaucomatous damage with IOP that is always within the normal
range. Vascular factors such as low blood pressure at night, migraine and Raynaud's phenomenon may
play a role.

Laser and surgery in glaucoma
Selective laser trabeculoplasty (SLT) treats the trabecular meshwork to increase outflow in openangle glaucoma and ocular hypertension. It can be repeated.
Laser peripheral iridotomy relieves pupil block in angle closure (see the iridotomy section).
Laser iridoplasty contracts the peripheral iris to pull it away from the angle, mainly for plateau iris or
an attack that does not respond to medicine.
Cyclodiode laser reduces aqueous production by treating the ciliary body. Conventional
continuous-wave treatment is used for eyes with a poor visual outlook or after other treatments have
failed; micropulse treatment is sometimes used earlier.
Trabeculectomy creates a guarded channel from the anterior chamber to a bleb under the
conjunctiva. Antifibrotic agents such as mitomycin C or 5-fluorouracil are used to reduce scarring. In
angle closure eyes the risk of aqueous misdirection is higher.
Tube shunts (such as Baerveldt, Ahmed or PAUL) drain aqueous to a plate placed further back on the
eye, often after failed trabeculectomy or in neovascular and uveitic glaucoma.
Minimally invasive glaucoma surgery (MIGS) uses small devices, often placed at the same time as
cataract surgery, for mild to moderate glaucoma.
Lens extraction deepens the anterior chamber and is an effective treatment for many people with
angle closure (see EAGLE above).
